paras: The Flushing tunnel fight was an armed clash on the night of October 23, 1903, near Flushing, Belmont County, Ohio, between a town marshal's posse and Black laborers, in which Marshal John G. Elliott was killed and four Black men were wounded. A crowd then threatened to lynch the captured men, and officials moved the prisoners to the county jail at St. Clairsville. Within four days an autopsy led authorities to suspect one of the marshal's own deputies, John Wheeler, of firing the fatal shot, and an Ohio paper headlined that the Black men were "Innocent."

The first Wheeling dispatch described the men as "a mob of angry negro laborers and foreigners" and placed the fight in the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad tunnel at Flushing. Dispatches from Flushing the next day said they belonged to a gang that had been robbing railroad laborers in camp and selling illicit whisky.

According to the first Wheeling dispatch, Elliott was called about 10 p.m. to quell a street disturbance, warned the men that a repetition would mean arrest, and was assaulted by two of them. He went for reinforcements, tracked the group to the railroad tunnel, and was shot through the heart while leading an attack; six of the men were captured by one account, three by another.

Around midnight three of the group were found in a cabin, answered a demand for surrender with gunfire, and were held there by the posse until county officers arrived. The wounded were named as William Smith, "shot through head" and listed as fatally wounded, and Ed Smith, Frank Williams and Edward Young, all described as "colored." On the morning of October 24 Sheriff Majors entered the barricaded house, removed three badly wounded men, and "had hard work to prevent the angry crowd from lynching them."
Four more people were arrested at noon, two of them Black women, and after citizens made "a hostile demonstration" officials slipped all the prisoners out to the St. Clairsville jail.

On October 27 a Flushing dispatch reported that, after an autopsy, John Wheeler, one of five men Elliott had deputized for the raid on "the camp of negro desperadoes," was suspected of firing the fatal shot. Wheeler had supplied the information behind the raid, and the shell that killed Elliott was said to have come from his gun; another posse member, Charles Bethel, arrested him as the marshal fell. Wheeler said the shooting was accidental, while an October 28 report said he had "deliberately murdered" Elliott, belonged to an illicit whisky gang, and was held under special guard amid "danger of lyching."
No report of William Smith's death, an inquest verdict, an indictment or a trial was found.

The story went out on the wire from Wheeling and ran from Alexandria and Savannah to Topeka, some papers placing Flushing in West Virginia. Western papers framed it as racial conflict, the Walla Walla Evening Statesman under "RAGE [race] WAR IN OHIO" and "White Citizens Threaten Lynching," the Seattle Star under "IN THROES OF RACE WAR." These first reports gave the officers' version as fact, calling the men a "gang" and a "mob" and stating that a Black man had shot the marshal.

The Stark County Democrat ran the first-day story as "NEGRO RIOT IN OHIO: One White Man Killed and Many Negroes Wounded," then on October 30 printed a Scripps-McRae telegram headed "INNOCENT: Negroes Did Not Kill Marshal In Flushing Riot." Weeklies such as the Cameron County Press kept printing the first-day account after the autopsy story appeared.

The only Black-press item found, in the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate of October 29, reprinted the autopsy dispatch under the headline "WAS A PLOT TO KILL MARSHAL ELLIOTT" and the deck "Flushing Town Officer Murdered by One of His Own Deputies."

Accounts of who killed Elliott shifted within days: the first reports said a Black man shot him through the back and escaped wounded, the autopsy reports pointed to deputy John Wheeler, and Belmont County officials named "Ed Wheeler, the negro now in jail here." That autopsy story rested on a "police theory" and still called Tom Templeton, a fugitive, "the supposed murderer," so the coverage does not settle who fired the shot.

reader.title: Flushing tunnel fight
bases: Town Marshal Elliott and men he deputized, joined by a citizens' posse, besieged and fought a group of Black laborers, leaving four Black men wounded and William Smith reported fatally hurt, after which a crowd threatened to lynch the prisoners (A1, A6, A4, A14).

William Smith was reported dying from wounds received in an armed fight with the marshal's deputized posse while being arrested (A1, A6, A14), and no death report was found; the crowd that threatened to lynch the prisoners was held off by the sheriff and the men were removed to St. Clairsville (A4, A9).

Separate Wheeling, Bellaire, Springfield and Flushing dispatches agree on the marshal's death, the wounding of several Black men and the lynching threat (A1, A9, A10, A4), though who fired the fatal shot is contested (A14, A16).

framing.detail: First reports presented the officers' version as fact and the Black men as a 'gang' and a 'mob,' under headlines such as 'RAGE [race] WAR IN OHIO' and 'IN THROES OF RACE WAR'.
Most papers ran short Wheeling or Bellaire wire items ('Desperate Fight in a Tunnel', 'Terror Reigns'), some placing Flushing in West Virginia.
The Stark County Democrat ran 'NEGRO RIOT IN OHIO: One White Man Killed' and three days later 'INNOCENT: Negroes Did Not Kill Marshal'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate printed only the autopsy dispatch, headed 'Was a Plot to Kill Marshal Elliott' and 'Murdered by One of His Own Deputies'.

conflicts.note: The autopsy reports are later and rest on physical evidence (the shell and the gun), but they also name Templeton as the supposed murderer; the St. Clairsville dispatch of the same day names a different Wheeler as Black. The coverage does not settle it.
